WITH pairs AS (                        -- every opportunity that existed at each cut-off
  SELECT m.month_end, (m.month_end + 1)::timestamptz AS cutoff,
         o.opportunity_id, o.stage, o.amount, o.owner_id
  FROM report_months m
  JOIN opportunities o ON o.created_at < (m.month_end + 1)::timestamptz
), h AS (
  SELECT * FROM opportunity_field_history
  WHERE field IN ('StageName', 'Amount', 'OwnerId')
), before_cut AS (                     -- last change strictly before the cut-off
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field)
         p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field, h.new_value AS v
  FROM pairs p JOIN h ON h.opportunity_id = p.opportunity_id AND h.changed_at < p.cutoff
  ORDER BY p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field, h.changed_at DESC, h.history_id DESC
), after_cut AS (                      -- first change at or after it: its old_value held before
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field)
         p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field, h.old_value AS v
  FROM pairs p JOIN h ON h.opportunity_id = p.opportunity_id AND h.changed_at >= p.cutoff
  ORDER BY p.month_end, p.opportunity_id, h.field, h.changed_at, h.history_id
), asof AS (
  SELECT p.month_end, p.opportunity_id,
         COALESCE(MAX(b.v) FILTER (WHERE b.field = 'StageName'),
                  MAX(a.v) FILTER (WHERE a.field = 'StageName'), MAX(p.stage))            AS stage,
         COALESCE(MAX(b.v) FILTER (WHERE b.field = 'Amount')::numeric,
                  MAX(a.v) FILTER (WHERE a.field = 'Amount')::numeric, MAX(p.amount))     AS amount,
         COALESCE(MAX(b.v) FILTER (WHERE b.field = 'OwnerId'),
                  MAX(a.v) FILTER (WHERE a.field = 'OwnerId'), MAX(p.owner_id))           AS owner_id
  FROM pairs p
  LEFT JOIN before_cut b ON b.month_end = p.month_end AND b.opportunity_id = p.opportunity_id
  LEFT JOIN after_cut  a ON a.month_end = p.month_end AND a.opportunity_id = p.opportunity_id
  GROUP BY p.month_end, p.opportunity_id
)
SELECT month_end, stage, owner_id,
       COUNT(*)    AS open_opportunities,
       SUM(amount) AS open_amount
FROM asof
WHERE stage NOT IN ('Closed Won', 'Closed Lost')
GROUP BY month_end, stage, owner_id
ORDER BY month_end, stage, owner_id;

Explanation. The value of a field at a cut-off is the new_value of the last change strictly before it. When there is none, the field still had its original value, and the history says what that was: the old_value of the first change after the cut-off. Only when the field never changed is the current value right. The query pairs each month-end with the opportunities created before its cut-off (an opportunity created later would otherwise pick up its original values and appear in a month in which it did not exist), finds the two candidate changes per field with DISTINCT ON, and pivots the three fields with FILTER. The two LEFT JOINs multiply rows per opportunity, but MAX per field is unaffected, because each (field, side) has at most one value. Closed stages are removed after reconstruction, so a deal that closes and reopens counts in exactly the months it was open. history_id breaks ties between changes in the same second.

Complexity. For M month-ends, O opportunities and H history rows, the joins are O(M · H) before DISTINCT ON sorts them; with an index on (opportunity_id, field, changed_at) each lookup is a short index range. In production one would compute validity intervals once (valid_from = changed_at, valid_to = LEAD(changed_at)) and join cut-offs to intervals.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery have no DISTINCT ON: use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY month_end, opportunity_id, field ORDER BY changed_at DESC, history_id DESC) = 1. Snowflake's ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (h.changed_at < p.cutoff) expresses the "last change before" lookup directly. BigQuery: DATE_ADD(month_end, INTERVAL 1 DAY) cast to TIMESTAMP is UTC; COUNTIF. Spark SQL: max_by(new_value, struct(changed_at, history_id)) over the filtered join. MySQL 8: ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE and MAX(CASE WHEN field = … THEN v END) for the pivot.

Edge cases built into the data. An opportunity whose first change comes after the first month-end (fallback to old_value); opportunities whose fields never change (current value); deals closed mid-window. Hard: owner changes, untracked fields (CloseDate, NextStep) in the same table, opportunities created during the window. Very Hard: a stage change at exactly 00:00:00 on the 1st, two stage changes in the same second, a deal closed in the first month and reopened in a later one.

Common mistakes. Using current values; taking only the history and dropping opportunities without an earlier change; using the new_value of the first later change instead of its old_value; <= at the cut-off; forgetting created_at; not filtering field, so a CloseDate change is read as a stage; filtering closed opportunities by their current stage; ties on changed_at without history_id; casting amount text after summing.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Reconstruction is exact as long as history is complete; snapshots are cheap to query and survive history retention, but freeze any errors and need a backfill that is itself a reconstruction. A strong answer does both: reconstruct to backfill and to audit, snapshot going forward. (2) A pipeline report usually converts at a stated rate (the month-end rate, or the planning rate) and says which; mixing the rate at close with the amount at month-end produces numbers nobody can reproduce. (3) Detect the gap: if the earliest retained change for an object is after the cut-off and the record existed before it, mark the value as "reconstructed from fallback" or unknown rather than trusting it. (4) Partition history by org and month of changed_at, cluster by (opportunity_id, field, changed_at); precompute validity intervals so as-of becomes a range join.

Rubric anchors. 2: rebuilds the stage from history but uses current owner or amount, or drops opportunities with no earlier change. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains validity intervals, snapshot versus reconstruction, and how to notice history that no longer reaches back far enough.

Strong signals. Asks what the value was before the first recorded change; checks the chain property (old_value equals previous new_value); tests the midnight boundary deliberately. Red flags. Assumes the history contains a row for every opportunity at creation; groups by the current owner "because ownership rarely changes".

WITH RECURSIVE grp AS (                -- walk from each survivor out to everything merged into it
  SELECT l.lead_id, l.lead_id AS root
  FROM leads l
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lead_merges m WHERE m.merged_lead_id = l.lead_id)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.merged_lead_id, g.root
  FROM lead_merges m
  JOIN grp g ON m.surviving_lead_id = g.lead_id
), starts AS (
  SELECT g.root, MIN(l.created_at) AS start_at
  FROM grp g JOIN leads l ON l.lead_id = g.lead_id
  GROUP BY g.root
), judged AS (
  SELECT COALESCE(s.lead_source, 'Unknown') AS lead_source,
         s.converted_at IS NOT NULL
           AND s.converted_at <= st.start_at + interval '30 days' AS converted
  FROM starts st
  JOIN leads s ON s.lead_id = st.root
  WHERE st.start_at + interval '30 days' <= timestamptz '{{as_of}}'
)
SELECT lead_source,
       COUNT(*)                                AS leads,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE converted)       AS converted_30d,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE converted)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS conversion_rate
FROM judged
GROUP BY lead_source
ORDER BY lead_source;

Explanation. Entity resolution comes first: the recursive CTE starts from survivors (leads never merged away) and follows the merge table backwards, so every lead, however many hops away, carries the id of its final survivor. Everything else is per group: the start is the minimum created_at across the group, the source and conversion are the survivor's. Maturity is judged on the group's start, so a group whose 30-day window is still open at the snapshot is not counted at all; counting it as unconverted biases recent cohorts downward. The rate is a numeric division rounded to 4 places.

Complexity. The recursion runs once per merge hop; with an index on lead_merges(surviving_lead_id) it is O(L + M) for L leads and M merges, then one hash aggregate. Real merge chains are short; the cost is dominated by the scan of leads.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and Spark SQL (3.4+ on Databricks) support recursive CTEs with similar syntax; BigQuery supports WITH RECURSIVE too. Without recursion (older Spark, some engines) resolve chains iteratively in the pipeline or with a fixed number of self-joins sized to the maximum chain length, and assert that no chain is longer. MySQL 8 has WITH RECURSIVE and TIMESTAMPADD(DAY, 30, start_at); SUM(converted) replaces FILTER. BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_ADD(start_at, INTERVAL 30 DAY), COUNTIF.

Edge cases built into the data. A person whose first lead came 10–20 days before the surviving lead, converting within 30 days of the survivor but not of the first lead (every level); duplicates from different sources; survivors that are not the earliest lead. Hard: groups younger than 30 days at the snapshot, a group that starts exactly 30 days before it (included), a conversion at exactly 30 days. Very Hard: a three-lead chain merged in two steps, survivors with no source.

Common mistakes. Counting lead records instead of groups; starting the clock at the survivor's own created_at; resolving merges one hop deep; counting immature groups as unconverted; strict < at the boundary; dropping NULL sources through an inner join on a source table; integer division; first-touch source when the specification says survivor.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Model merges as events with an undone_at (or a separate unmerge event) and resolve groups as of a date; reports for earlier dates must be recomputed or explicitly frozen, and a strong answer says which. (2) Compute groups once (a table of lead_id → root, with start_at, first_source, survivor_source) and let each report choose the attribution column; the logic lives in one place. (3) Estimate duplicates with a matching rule (normalised email, phone) and report the rate as a range between "records" and "probable people", stating the rule. (4) Maintain a union-find style mapping table updated from the day's merges only; a new merge re-roots one group, so only that group's rows change.

Rubric anchors. 2: folds duplicates one level deep but measures from the survivor, or counts young groups. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses unmerges as of a date, attribution as a column rather than a fork, and incremental resolution.

Strong signals. Asks "is a merged lead still a lead?" before writing SQL; spots the maturity bias without prompting. Red flags. Deduplicates by email inside the report instead of using the merge log; treats the survivor's creation as the person's first contact.

WITH first_response AS (
  SELECT case_id, MIN(created_at) AS responded_at
  FROM case_comments
  WHERE author_type = 'agent' AND is_public
  GROUP BY case_id
), spans AS (
  SELECT c.case_id, c.priority, e.response_minutes * 60 AS target_s, e.calendar,
         c.created_at AS s,
         COALESCE(f.responded_at, timestamptz '{{as_of}}') AS t,   -- unanswered: measure to the snapshot
         f.responded_at IS NOT NULL AS answered
  FROM cases c
  JOIN entitlements e ON e.priority = c.priority
  LEFT JOIN first_response f ON f.case_id = c.case_id
), measured AS (
  SELECT sp.*,
         CASE WHEN sp.calendar = '24x7' THEN EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM sp.t - sp.s)
              ELSE COALESCE((
                SELECT SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM LEAST(sp.t, d + make_interval(hours => {{close}}))
                                            - GREATEST(sp.s, d + make_interval(hours => {{open}}))))
                FROM generate_series(date_trunc('day', sp.s), date_trunc('day', sp.t), interval '1 day') AS d
                WHERE EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM d) < 6
                  AND d::date NOT IN (SELECT holiday_date FROM holidays)
                  AND LEAST(sp.t, d + make_interval(hours => {{close}}))
                      > GREATEST(sp.s, d + make_interval(hours => {{open}}))
              ), 0)
         END AS business_s
  FROM spans sp
), judged AS (
  SELECT priority, answered AND business_s <= target_s AS met
  FROM measured
  WHERE answered OR business_s > target_s          -- unanswered and still within target: not judged
)
SELECT priority,
       COUNT(*)                          AS cases,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE met)       AS met,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT met)   AS breached,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE met)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS met_rate
FROM judged
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY priority;

Explanation. Business time is the measure of the intersection between the case's interval and the calendar's windows. Because a window never crosses midnight here, the calendar decomposes into one window per business day, and the correlated subquery sums the positive overlaps of the days the interval touches. Creation and response outside business hours need no special casing: the overlap clips them to the window. Unanswered cases are measured to the snapshot; if they are already over target they are breaches, otherwise they are not judged yet. A 24x7 entitlement is plain elapsed seconds. The first response is filtered on both author type and visibility, because automated acknowledgements usually arrive first and internal notes are not seen by the customer.

Complexity. One generated row per case-day: O(Σ case durations in days). Fine for a report over weeks; for years of cases, precompute a calendar table with cumulative business seconds at each day's start (and the window bounds), so business time between two instants is cum(t) − cum(s) with clipping on the two end days: O(1) per case after two lookups.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: no generate_series over timestamps; join to a calendar table (or TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n)) with DATEADD), DAYOFWEEKISO, DATEDIFF('second', a, b). BigQuery: UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(DATE(s), DATE(t))), EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK …) is 1 = Sunday, TIMESTAMP_DIFF(b, a, SECOND). Spark SQL: explode(sequence(to_date(s), to_date(t))), dayofweek is 1 = Sunday. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE or a calendar table; TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, a, b). In every engine a persisted calendar table is the production answer.

Edge cases built into the data. A response at exactly the target (met) and one second later (breached), both from cases opened on a weekend, a holiday or outside the day's hours; replies sent outside business hours; customer comments before the agent's reply. Hard: automated acknowledgements within seconds of creation, internal notes before the first public reply, an old unanswered case (breached), a case opened minutes before the snapshot (not judged), a second holiday. Very Hard: P1 on a 24x7 calendar, including a case opened on Friday evening.

Common mistakes. Wall-clock subtraction; counting the customer's or the automated comment as the response; ignoring holidays; < at the target; dropping unanswered cases (hides the worst breaches) or counting all of them as breached (punishes cases that are not due); applying business hours to a 24x7 entitlement; clipping only the start or only the end of the interval; joining comments without aggregating first, which duplicates cases.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Store each calendar's windows as UTC intervals generated from its local rules (with DST), assign each case a calendar from its entitlement or region, and intersect with that calendar's intervals; never convert the case to local time and reuse a UTC rule. (2) A table (calendar_id, day, window_start, window_end, cum_before) makes elapsed time cum(t) − cum(s), where cum(x) = cum_before(day(x)) + clip(x − window_start, 0, window length). (3) Model status changes as intervals; the clock runs only on intervals where the status is "running", intersected with business windows: the same overlap sum, over more intervals. (4) Breach time for open cases is "created + target in business time", precomputed once per case; the minute-by-minute view is a comparison with now, while the compliance report stays batch.

Rubric anchors. 2: business time computed, but weekends handled and holidays ignored, or the first response wrongly defined, or unanswered cases mishandled. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also designs the cumulative calendar table and handles time zones and pauses correctly in discussion.

Strong signals. Draws the interval-on-calendar picture before writing SQL; asks what happens to unanswered cases; tests a weekend-spanning case by hand. Red flags. Converts business time with a fixed ratio (e.g. "8/24 of elapsed"); treats the snapshot time as the response for unanswered cases and calls them met.

def visible_counts(roles, users, records, no_hierarchy):
    off = set(no_hierarchy)
    parent = dict(roles)
    children = {r: [] for r in parent}
    roots = []
    for r, p in roles:
        if p is None:
            roots.append(r)
        else:
            children[p].append(r)
    role_of = dict(users)
    own = {u: 0 for u, _ in users}
    here = {r: 0 for r in parent}            # shareable records owned by users in exactly this role
    for _, obj, owner in records:
        own[owner] += 1
        r = role_of[owner]
        if r is not None and obj not in off:
            here[r] += 1
    order, stack = [], roots[:]              # iterative pre-order: parents before children
    while stack:
        r = stack.pop()
        order.append(r)
        stack.extend(children[r])
    sub = dict(here)                         # shareable records owned at or below each role
    for r in reversed(order):                # every child is finished before its parent
        p = parent[r]
        if p is not None:
            sub[p] += sub[r]
    return {u: own[u] + (sub[r] - here[r] if r is not None else 0) for u, r in users}

Explanation. What a user sees through the hierarchy depends only on their role: the shareable records owned strictly below it. So the work is per role, and a subtree sum is a post-order fold: each role's total is its own count plus its children's totals. A pre-order built with an explicit stack lists every parent before its descendants; walking it in reverse finishes every child first, with no recursion (the test tree is thousands of levels deep). "Strictly below" is the subtree total minus the role's own count, which is how peers in one role are kept out of each other's counts. Each user adds their own records of every object, including objects that do not share through the hierarchy; users without a role get only their own.

Complexity. O(R + U + N) time and O(R + U) memory for R roles, U users, N records. The timing test (12 000 roles about 6 000 levels deep, 30 000 users, 120 000 records) runs in about 0.4 s in CPython. Walking each role's subtree with an explicit stack and memoising per role took about 12.5 s on the same input; a per-user walk without memoisation, or any recursive version, is worse (or raises RecursionError).

Dialect notes. In SQL this is a recursive CTE producing (ancestor, descendant) pairs, which is O(R × depth) rows on a deep tree; a closure table maintained on change, or a materialised path (/ceo/vp/dir/) with prefix matching, is the usual production shape. In Java or Go the same two passes apply; Java's default thread stack also overflows on deep recursion. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Peers in one role; a grand-manager; an empty middle role; two separate trees; a user who owns nothing; (Hard) a user with no role, and roles listed child-first; (Very Hard) an object excluded from hierarchy sharing, including one nobody owns.

Common mistakes. Counting peers (using "at or below" for the user's own role); recursion that fails on the deep test; assuming roles is listed parents-first; counting the user's own records twice (once as owner, once as "in their role"); dropping excluded-object records from the owner's own count; building sets of record ids per role; forgetting users with zero visible records.

Follow-up guidance. (1) For one record, walk up from the owner's role to the root collecting users in each ancestor role: O(depth + users found); precompute nothing. (2) Expand each rule into (grantee role subtree) × (owner role subtree) and count distinct records per user with a bitmap or by deduplicating grants per (user, record); a strong answer notes that union of grants is not a sum. (3) Moving a subtree changes totals only on the old and new ancestor paths: subtract its total along the old path, add it along the new one, O(depth). (4) Partition by org, cap per-task work by role count, store per-role here and sub so one user's count is explainable as "own + sum below role X".

Rubric anchors. 2: correct on shallow trees but per-user walks, recursion, or peers counted. 3: passes all tests with an iterative post-order sum. 4: also explains per-record lookup, rule expansion without double counting and O(depth) updates for a move.

Strong signals. Notices that the answer is per role before writing code; asks about depth and recursion limits; checks the peer rule with a two-user example. Red flags. Raising the recursion limit as the fix; claiming this rule is how a particular product's sharing works in full.

import heapq


def route_cases(agents, events):
    n = len(agents)
    index = {a: i for i, (a, _, _) in enumerate(agents)}
    skills = [s for _, s, _ in agents]
    cap = [c for _, _, c in agents]
    load = [0] * n
    last = [-1] * n                 # time of the latest assignment; -1 = never (times are >= 0)
    online = [True] * n
    ver = [0] * n                   # bumped on every change; older heap entries are stale
    heaps = {}

    def publish(i):
        ver[i] += 1
        if online[i]:
            entry = (load[i] - cap[i], last[i], i, ver[i])     # most spare, longest idle, input order
            for s in skills[i]:
                heapq.heappush(heaps.setdefault(s, []), entry)

    for i in range(n):
        publish(i)
    held, out = {}, {}
    for ev in events:
        kind = ev[0]
        if kind == 'case':
            _, t, cid, skill, units = ev
            h = heaps.get(skill, [])
            chosen = None
            while h:
                neg_spare, _, i, v = h[0]
                if v != ver[i]:                                # stale (or offline): drop lazily
                    heapq.heappop(h)
                    continue
                if -neg_spare >= units:                        # the top has the most spare capacity
                    chosen = i
                break
            out[cid] = None if chosen is None else agents[chosen][0]
            if chosen is not None:
                load[chosen] += units
                last[chosen] = t
                held[cid] = (chosen, units)
                publish(chosen)
        elif kind == 'done':
            got = held.pop(ev[2], None)
            if got is not None:
                load[got[0]] -= got[1]
                publish(got[0])
        else:
            i = index[ev[2]]
            online[i] = kind == 'online'
            publish(i)
    return out

Explanation. The routing rule is a lexicographic maximum: most spare capacity, then oldest latest assignment, then input position, which as a min-heap key is (load − capacity, last, position). Every event changes at most one agent, but that agent may sit in several skill heaps, and Python's heap has no decrease-key. So each change bumps the agent's version and pushes a fresh entry into every heap the agent belongs to; an entry whose version is old is discarded when it surfaces. Going offline is just a version bump without a push, and coming online pushes again. Once the top valid entry cannot fit the case, no agent can, because it has the most spare capacity; the case gets None. Completions free capacity only for routed cases.

Complexity. Each event pushes at most k entries (k skills per agent) and every entry is popped at most once: O(E · k · log(E · k)) time, O(E · k) memory in the worst case. The timing test (2 000 agents, 60 000 cases, about 120 000 events) runs in about 0.4–0.7 s in CPython. Scanning the agents with the skill for every case took about 15–19 s on the same input.

Dialect notes. Java: PriorityQueue<long[]> per skill with a version array, or a TreeSet per skill keyed by (−spare, last, idx) with remove-and-reinsert (O(log n) without stale entries). C++: std::set per skill for the same. Go: container/heap with an index field supports heap.Fix for true decrease-key. In SQL this is sequential state and does not belong in a query. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Most spare beats input order; a never-assigned agent beats one assigned earlier; equal spare broken by oldest assignment, then input order; no agent with the skill; everyone full until a completion; (Hard) a free agent without the skill, a completion for an unrouted case; (Very Hard) units exactly equal to spare, spare capacity spread over agents that does not add up, an agent offline while a case completes and back online.

Common mistakes. Choosing the first agent with room; least-recently-completed instead of latest assignment; ties broken by agent id instead of input position; updating only one skill heap; trusting a stale top entry; scanning past the top to find one that "fits" (the top has the most room, so nothing below fits either); freeing capacity for a done of an unrouted case (a KeyError, or worse, negative load); keeping offline agents eligible.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep a FIFO per skill; on every capacity increase, for each of the agent's skills, offer the head of that queue if it fits; a strong answer notices starvation of large cases behind small ones and names a policy (strict FIFO or skip-ahead). (2) Least-active ignores capacity: an agent with capacity 5 and 2 in progress loses to one with capacity 1 and 1 in progress; most-available spreads by headroom, least-active by count. (3) A heap per (skill, level) with a query over levels ≥ L, or a segment tree over levels whose leaves are heaps; with ten levels, ten heap tops is enough. (4) Make capacity a reservation with compare-and-set (or one owner per agent's state), and retry with the next candidate when the reservation fails.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct rule but a scan per case, or one heap that ignores multiple skills. 3: passes every test with per-skill heaps and lazy invalidation. 4: also explains why the top test is enough, waiting queues without starvation, and how concurrency changes the design.

Strong signals. Writes the comparison key before any code; asks whether an unroutable case waits; tests an agent with two skills. Red flags. Re-sorting all agents on every event; presenting this rule as how a specific product's routing works.

def recalc_order(formulas, edits):
    readers = {}                      # field -> formulas that read it, each once
    pending = {}                      # formula -> distinct formula fields it reads
    for f, refs in formulas.items():
        distinct = set(refs)
        pending[f] = sum(1 for x in distinct if x in formulas)
        for x in distinct:
            readers.setdefault(x, []).append(f)
    level = {}
    layer = [f for f, n in pending.items() if n == 0]
    depth = 1
    while layer:                      # Kahn's algorithm, one layer per level
        nxt = []
        for f in layer:
            level[f] = depth
            for g in readers.get(f, ()):
                pending[g] -= 1
                if pending[g] == 0:
                    nxt.append(g)
        layer = nxt
        depth += 1
    if len(level) < len(formulas):
        return None                   # some formula is on, or behind, a cycle
    out = []
    for edit in edits:
        hit = set()
        stack = list(edit)
        while stack:
            for g in readers.get(stack.pop(), ()):
                if g not in hit:
                    hit.add(g)
                    stack.append(g)
        out.append(sorted(hit, key=lambda f: (level[f], f)))
    return out

Explanation. Build the reverse map once: for each field, the formulas that read it, each formula listed once even when its expression names the field twice. Kahn's algorithm, processed one layer at a time, assigns levels: the first layer is every formula with no formula inputs (level 1), and a formula joins the next layer when its last formula input is removed, which is exactly one more than the highest level among its inputs. Counting distinct formula inputs matters: a formula that names Net__c twice would otherwise wait for two removals that never come and look like a cycle. Any formula that never reaches in-degree zero is on a cycle or reads one, so the configuration is rejected with None before any save is answered, whether or not a save reaches the cycle. For each save, a walk over the reverse map from the edited fields collects every formula that can change, and sorting by (level, name) gives the order. Every formula's inputs have strictly lower levels, so the order is a valid evaluation order, and the name breaks ties so the answer is unique.

Complexity. O(V + E) once for the reverse map and the levels, then O(A + E_A + A log A) per save, where A is the number of affected formulas and E_A their outgoing references. The timing test (37 500 formulas, about 75 000 references, 3 000 saves, about 18 affected formulas per save) runs in about 0.2 s in CPython. A fixed point over every formula for every save takes about 0.08 s per save on the same data, about four minutes in total; a single topological pass over the whole configuration per save is O(saves · (V + E)) and still takes about a minute.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ use adjacency lists of ints after interning names, an int array of in-degrees and an explicit stack; sort affected ids with a comparator on (level, name). In SQL the affected set is a recursive CTE over a formula_reads(formula, field) table and the level a second recursive CTE with MAX; cycle detection needs a depth cap or PostgreSQL's CYCLE clause, and engines differ (Snowflake and BigQuery support recursive CTEs with iteration limits). Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A chain whose names sort opposite to its levels; a diamond (the shared formula once, after both parents); equal levels ordered by name; a formula that reads the edited field directly and a level-2 formula (level 3, not 1); levels taken from the whole configuration, not the edit; an edit no formula reads ([]); a two-field cycle (None); several saves in order; (Hard) a field read twice, a referenced name no formula defines, a twelve-level chain; (Very Hard) a self-reference, a cycle no save reaches, an empty save and a repeated field, no saves at all ([]).

Common mistakes. Ordering by distance from the edited field (BFS depth) instead of the global level; computing levels only over the affected subgraph; counting repeated references in the in-degree, which turns [X, X] into a false cycle; returning None only when a save reaches the cycle; including the edited input fields in the output; recursion depth errors on long chains (not exercised by the tests beyond twelve levels, but worth asking about); recomputing levels per save.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Cross-object references make the reverse map span objects: a parent field fans out to every child record. Plan per (object, field) once, then multiply by the child count; batch child updates and consider deferring them asynchronously with a freshness flag on the cached values. (2) Early cut-off: evaluate in level order and only enqueue a formula's readers when its value actually changed. The static order is still valid; the affected set becomes dynamic. (3) A changed formula only affects the levels of its descendants; recompute levels for the reachable subgraph, and note that adding a reference at the bottom of a long chain can raise thousands of levels. Reject cycles at save time of the metadata. (4) Cache the plan per (org, object, metadata version); invalidate on deploy by bumping the version, and precompute plans for frequent edit sets lazily.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct affected sets but the wrong order (alphabetical or BFS depth), or cycles missed; several edge tests fail. 3: all tests pass with levels computed once and a per-save walk. 4: also explains why (level, name) is a valid evaluation order, handles repeated references deliberately, states both complexities, and gives a credible answer on cross-object fan-out and early cut-off.

Strong signals. Asks whether the level is global or relative to the edit; asks what to do with a cycle no save reaches; mentions that Kahn's algorithm finds the cycle and the levels in one pass. Red flags. A fixed point per save defended as "graphs are small"; returning a partial order when there is a cycle.

def match_leads(accounts, leads, public_domains):
    owners = {}                                   # domain -> set of account ids
    for account_id, domains in accounts:
        for d in domains:
            owners.setdefault(d.strip().lower(), set()).add(account_id)
    public = {d.strip().lower() for d in public_domains}
    out = []
    for email in leads:
        _, at, domain = email.strip().rpartition("@")
        domain = domain.lower()
        if not at or not domain:
            out.append(None)                      # no @, or nothing after it
            continue
        best = None
        suffix = domain
        while True:                               # longest suffix first, one label at a time
            if suffix in public:
                best = None
                break
            if best is None and suffix in owners:
                best = owners[suffix]             # keep walking: a shorter public suffix still wins
            dot = suffix.find(".")
            if dot < 0:
                break
            suffix = suffix[dot + 1:]
        out.append(next(iter(best)) if best is not None and len(best) == 1 else None)
    return out

Explanation. Every account domain goes into a dict from normalised domain to the set of accounts that list it; a set makes a domain listed twice by one account count once. For a lead, rpartition("@") takes the text after the last @ and also tells you whether there was an @ at all. The suffixes of the lead's domain that start at a label boundary are the domain itself and each text after a dot. Walking them from longest to shortest, the first suffix an account claims is the longest matching account domain. The walk continues to the end anyway, because a shorter suffix may be a public domain (uk.yahoo.com claimed by an account, yahoo.com public), and the public rule wins. If the longest claimed suffix has more than one owner the lead is ambiguous and gets None, with no fallback to a shorter domain.

Complexity. Building the dict is O(total domain length). Each lead costs O(L²) character work for L labels in the worst case because each suffix is a new string, which is tiny for real domains; a trie of reversed labels gets O(L) but is slower in CPython. The timing test (40 000 accounts, about 80 000 domains, 150 000 leads) runs in about 0.6 s in CPython. Comparing every lead with every account domain is about 1.2 × 10¹⁰ endswith calls: about 0.02 s per lead, nearly an hour in total.

Dialect notes. In SQL, generate each lead's suffixes (split the domain into labels, then ARRAY_TO_STRING over a slice, or a recursive CTE), join to an account_domains table on equality, and keep the longest match per lead with ROW_NUMBER(); ambiguity is a COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) over the winning domain. A join on lead_domain LIKE '%' || account_domain is the naive scan and also matches across label boundaries. Snowflake has SPLIT and ARRAY_SLICE, BigQuery SPLIT and ARRAY_TO_STRING with offsets. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A subdomain of an account's domain; the longest domain winning over a parent; a look-alike (notacme.com) and a domain with the account's domain in the middle (acme.com.evil.net); a public domain also listed by an account; a domain listed twice by one account; mixed case and surrounding spaces in emails and in account domains; emails with no @, nothing after it, or only a bare domain; an empty public list; (Hard) the longest match listed between two others, a public domain in upper case; (Very Hard) an ambiguous longest domain with no fallback, a quoted local part containing @, a subdomain of a public domain.

Common mistakes. endswith(account_domain) without the dot, matching notacme.com; split("@")[1], which takes the wrong part with two @ signs and raises with none; stopping the walk at the first claimed suffix before checking shorter public suffixes; falling back to the parent account when the longest domain is ambiguous; counting the same account twice as ambiguity; forgetting to normalise account or public domains; a regex built from all account domains.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep the dict as a long-lived index updated from account change events (add and remove a domain with its account id); rebuild from scratch nightly as a check. (2) A curated "domain group" table linking domains, owned by a person or an approved data source, not inferred from string similarity (acme.co.uk and acme.com.au can be unrelated companies). (3) Log every match with its rule and the ambiguous candidates, then measure acceptance and re-assignment rates by owners before automating ambiguity; beware a rule that rewards owners with many open deals. (4) The algorithm and public list can be shared; account domains and leads are each org's own data and the index is per org.

Rubric anchors. 2: substring or endswith matching without label boundaries, or an O(n · m) scan. 3: all tests pass with suffix lookups. 4: also explains why the walk continues after the first match, defends "no fallback" for ambiguity, and handles freshness and multi-tenancy credibly.

Strong signals. Asks how to treat an ambiguous domain before coding; tests notacme.com unprompted. Red flags. Matching on substrings; "pick the first account" for ambiguity.

from bisect import bisect_right

BUCKETS = ("closed", "commit", "best_case", "pipeline")
ROLLS_INTO = {                      # forecast category -> buckets it counts in
    "Closed": ("closed", "commit", "best_case", "pipeline"),
    "Commit": ("commit", "best_case", "pipeline"),
    "Best Case": ("best_case", "pipeline"),
    "Pipeline": ("pipeline",),
    "Omitted": (),                                                    # fix 1: counts nowhere
}


def _fiscal_quarter(close_date, fy_start):
    year, month = int(close_date[:4]), int(close_date[5:7])
    fy = year + 1 if fy_start > 1 and month >= fy_start else year     # fix 5: the first month belongs to the new year
    quarter = (month - fy_start) % 12 // 3 + 1
    return "FY%d-Q%d" % (fy, quarter)


def forecast_rollup(opps, split_rows, rates, corporate, fy_start):
    by_currency = {}
    for currency, effective, ppm in rates:
        by_currency.setdefault(currency, []).append((effective, ppm))
    for series in by_currency.values():
        series.sort()
    dates = {c: [d for d, _ in s] for c, s in by_currency.items()}
    splits = {}
    for opp_id, user, pct in split_rows:
        splits.setdefault(opp_id, []).append((user, pct))             # fix 3: keep every member

    out = {}
    for o in opps:
        if o["currency"] == corporate:
            ppm = 1_000_000
        else:
            i = bisect_right(dates[o["currency"]], o["close_date"]) - 1   # fix 2: a rate effective on the close date applies
            ppm = by_currency[o["currency"]][i][1]
        owner = max(o["owner_history"])[1]                            # fix 4: the latest change by date
        credits = splits.get(o["id"], [(owner, 100)])
        quarter = _fiscal_quarter(o["close_date"], fy_start)
        for user, pct in credits:
            amount = o["amount"] * pct * ppm // 100_000_000
            row = out.setdefault(user + "/" + quarter, dict.fromkeys(BUCKETS, 0))
            for bucket in ROLLS_INTO[o["category"]]:
                row[bucket] += amount
    return out

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Omitted rolls into pipeline. ROLLS_INTO["Omitted"] is ("pipeline",). Symptom: deals reps marked Omitted still inflate the pipeline. Fix: (). The row still exists, as the specification requires.
  2. Rate effective on the close date ignored. bisect_left(dates, close) - 1 gives the last rate strictly before the close date. Symptom: a deal closing on the day a new rate takes effect is converted at the old rate; for a close date equal to the earliest rate it even wraps to index −1, the newest rate. Fix: bisect_right(...) - 1.
  3. Split rows overwrite each other. The dict comprehension keeps one (user, pct) per opportunity, the last row. Symptom: on a split deal only one member is credited, with their percent, and the total credited is less than the deal. Fix: collect a list of rows per opportunity.
  4. Owner taken from list order. owner_history[-1] assumes the history is sorted by date, and the export is not. Symptom: some reassigned deals still count for the previous owner. Fix: the change with the latest date, max(owner_history)[1] (dates are distinct).
  5. First fiscal month in the previous year. month > fy_start puts the first month of a fiscal year that starts after January in the old fiscal year (the quarter number is still right). Symptom: February deals with a February fiscal year land in last year's Q1, mixing with the previous February. Fix: month >= fy_start.

Each bug has its own check (an Omitted deal, a rate effective on the close date, a two-way split, an unsorted owner history, a February close with fy_start = 2), and fixing the other four leaves exactly that check (and some samples) failing. The Medium samples have a single owner, no splits and a January fiscal year, so they pass on the original code; the Hard and Very Hard samples fail until several bugs are fixed.

Explanation. The rollup is a pure function of four inputs: who gets credit (splits, else the current owner), how much in corporate currency (the dated rate on the close date, rounded down per credited user), which period (the fiscal quarter, named by the year the fiscal year ends), and which buckets (the cumulative category rule). Each bug breaks exactly one of them, and the symptoms are what a sales operations team would actually report.

Complexity. O(r log r) to sort rates, O(n log r) for the lookups, linear in split rows. The timing test (60 000 opportunities, 16 000 rates) runs in about 0.6 s in CPython.

Dialect notes. In SQL the dated rate is an as-of join: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ppm FROM rates r WHERE r.currency = o.currency AND r.effective_date <= o.close_date ORDER BY r.effective_date DESC LIMIT 1) in PostgreSQL, ASOF JOIN in Snowflake, a QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() in BigQuery. The same < versus <= bug appears there. The fiscal year is EXTRACT(YEAR FROM close_date) + CASE WHEN fy_start > 1 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM close_date) >= fy_start THEN 1 ELSE 0 END. Integer division of a product needs NUMERIC or BIGINT, never FLOAT. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A Closed deal in every bucket and a Pipeline deal only in pipeline; Omitted deals keeping a zero row; a rate effective on the close date and one effective the day after; a two-way split of an odd amount rounded down per member; an owner history out of date order; a February close with a February fiscal year, and 31 January in the previous year's Q4; a November fiscal year across the calendar year; the corporate currency converting at exactly 1 even when a rate is listed for it.

Common mistakes. Fixing bisect by sorting rates descending and introducing a new off-by-one; dropping Omitted rows entirely (the specification keeps the row); rounding the converted amount before splitting, which double-rounds; sorting owner_history in place (it mutates the caller's data, though harmless here); "fixing" the fiscal year by naming it by the start year; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Snapshot the inputs or the output: store the weekly rollup with the input versions (opportunity history as of Friday, the rate table version, the split rows), or rebuild from field history and effective-dated rates as of that timestamp. (2) Only rows whose close dates fall on or after the late rate's effective date and before the next rate change; recompute them, keep both versions and show leaders a change note. (3) Reject or quarantine at import with a validation that percents sum to 100 per opportunity; do not silently scale. (4) Replace the arithmetic with a lookup into a per-org fiscal calendar table of periods (start date, end date, year, quarter), which also handles 4-4-5 and 13-period calendars.

Rubric anchors. 2: finds two or three bugs, some checks still fail. 3: all five fixed with minimal changes, all checks pass, each explained. 4: also names each business symptom, explains the bisect_left wrap-around to index −1, adds a regression test per bug, and answers the reproducibility follow-up with versioned inputs.

Strong signals. Reproduces each complaint with a one-opportunity case; reads the bisect boundary carefully. Red flags. Converting with floats "to be safe"; changing the output format; deleting the Omitted category from the output.

SFC-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Connectors. A connector framework with a small contract per source type: pull (scheduled incremental queries against an API or warehouse with a stored high-water mark plus an overlap window), push (a streaming ingestion API with an event key, event time and an idempotency key per batch), and file drops (object-storage notifications). Credentials live in a per-org secret store, never in mappings. Retries are bounded with backoff; a connector that keeps failing is paused and the org administrator is told why.
  • Raw landing. Every delivery lands raw and immutable under org / source / ingest_date / batch, with a manifest row: org, source, batch id, content hash, row count, schema fingerprint, received time. A redelivered file with the same hash is a no-op; a renamed copy of the same content is caught by the hash; a changed file for the same period is a new version. Streams land per org in a partitioned log, keyed by org and source so one org's replay stays on its own partitions.
  • Mapping and transformation. Each org's mapping (source field to common-model field, with typed transformations) is stored as versioned configuration. A mapping save is validated (types, a dry run on a sample of the org's recent raw rows, alarms for suspicious changes such as a field mapped to a different semantic type) before it becomes active. The transformer reads raw batches and writes common-model tables, stamping every row with org_id, source_id, source_key, source_ts, mapping_version, batch_id. A mapping change triggers a replay of the affected sources from raw data, written to a new version and swapped atomically per org and source.
  • Common-model storage. Lakehouse tables partitioned by org (and by date for events), with upserts keyed by (org, source, source_key) and ordered by source_ts then batch id, so replays and late events converge. Two sources describing the same order stay separate rows with their source.
  • Deletions. Explicit delete events become tombstones. For full extracts, keys absent from today's extract become deletion candidates only if the extract passed sanity checks (row count within a band of the previous one, schema unchanged); otherwise the batch is held for review. Tombstones are applied within a day and propagated to downstream consumers as delete events.
  • Freshness. Per org and source: the age of the newest row queryable in the common model, from event ingestion time for streams and from file arrival for batch, compared with {fast_freshness} and {batch_freshness}. Shown to administrators with the last successful batch, rows in and rows rejected, and the reason for any delay.
  • Isolation and fairness. Every key and path starts with org id; queries are scoped by the platform, not by the client. Shared compute uses per-org quotas and separate queues for streaming and backfill work, so a backfill gets leftover capacity, never the streaming path's.

Competing designs to accept. A streaming-first design (everything through the log, files turned into events); a batch-first lakehouse with micro-batches for streams; ELT where raw data lands in the warehouse and mappings are SQL views materialised per org (accept if mapping versions and replays are explicit). Each is fine if idempotency, versioned mappings and per-org fairness hold.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Small files from many small orgs; a single shared queue where backfills starve streams; mappings applied in place with no version, making errors unrepairable; deletions by absence on truncated files; schema drift silently writing nulls; freshness measured as queue lag rather than from the source's view.

Incident guidance.

  • Renamed duplicate file for 300 orgs: the content hash catches it if checked per org and source; if rows already doubled, they share source keys, so the upsert should have absorbed them; doubling means some pipeline appended instead of merging. Identify affected batches from the manifest, delete the duplicate batch's rows by batch id and replay. Add hash checks independent of file names and a row-count anomaly alarm per source.
  • One org's backfill pushes others past {fast_freshness}: backfill and streaming must use separate queues and quotas; throttle the backfill to its quota, let streaming catch up, and alert on per-org freshness, not only global lag. Long term, schedule large backfills on separate capacity.
  • Phone mapped into email: the mapping save should have failed validation (values that do not parse as emails). Revert to the previous mapping version, replay the affected source from raw for that window, emit corrections downstream, and ask identity resolution to undo merges made with the bad values (their edges carry the source and mapping version). Add semantic validation and a staged rollout for mapping changes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Replay from raw with the corrected mapping version into a shadow table, swap atomically, and publish a change notice; at {daily_records} a day estimate the replay window and prioritise recent data. (2) Additive columns flow in as unmapped; renamed or retyped columns stop the affected mapping with a clear error rather than writing nulls; dates parsed with an explicit per-source format. (3) No: hold the batch, alert, and require confirmation or a second consistent extract before deleting. (4) Separate backfill queue, per-org quotas and priorities. (5) A deletion ledger per request with each table's confirmation and the time it applied.

Rubric anchors. 2: connectors write straight into common tables; no raw retention, no mapping versions, freshness only as a global lag. 3: immutable raw landing with idempotency, versioned mappings stamped on rows, replay for remaps, deletions from events and absence, per-source freshness, per-org isolation. 4: also guards against truncated extracts, mapping validation and staged rollout, separate backfill capacity, and crisp incident responses.

Strong signals. Asks how a full extract signals deletion; stamps rows with mapping versions without being prompted. Red flags. "Overwrite with the latest file"; isolation by client-side filters; one global queue for all orgs.

SFC-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Events. Each run emits run_started, element events (element_id, type, start offset, duration, outcome, queries and DML rows used) and run_finished with outcome, total duration, limit use, flow id and version, org id, triggering record id and object, the record ids it changed and the trigger type. Faults carry the element, an error class, a message template with record ids but no field values, and the limit that was hit if any. Values are excluded by an allowlist of fields that telemetry may contain, not a denylist.
  • Chain identity. Each save gets a chain_id; every run gets run_id, parent_run_id and a depth. The transaction context carries them, and any asynchronous work (queued jobs, scheduled paths, platform events) stores the chain context in its message, so a step two hours later continues the same chain. A chain also records why each run started (record changed by run X, event published by run Y).
  • Emission. The runtime writes events to a bounded in-memory buffer per application server and a background shipper sends them in batches to a durable log. If the buffer is full, events are dropped and a drop counter (per org and outcome) is shipped; saves never wait. Faults and slow runs go to a priority buffer so they are dropped last.
  • Transport and processing. A partitioned log keyed by org id (large orgs spread by flow id). A stream processor builds per-minute aggregates per (org, flow, version, element): run counts by outcome, duration sketches for percentiles, limit use, fault counts by class. Exact counts come from all runs, including sampled-out ones, because counting happens before sampling.
  • Sampling and storage. Keep all faulted, slow (above a per-flow threshold) and limit-stopped runs in full detail; sample fast successes per flow at a rate that keeps the volume of {daily_runs} affordable, with the sampling rate stored so estimates can be scaled. Detail is kept {detail_retention} in a columnar store partitioned by org and day; aggregates are kept for 13 months. A per-record index (org, record id, time) points to chains that touched the record.
  • Administrator views. For one record: the chains that changed it, as a tree of runs with elements and timings. For one flow: runs, faults, p50/p95 by version and element. For the org: top flows by time, fault rate and limit use, and loops (chains hitting the {max_depth}-level limit).
  • Privacy and isolation. Every row has org id; the query service enforces it. Field-value capture is an explicit, time-boxed debug session per flow or user, with an expiry enforced by the platform, an audit record and a separate store with short retention.

Competing designs to accept. OpenTelemetry-style traces with spans per run and element, exported to a tracing backend with tail-based sampling; event logs into a lakehouse with batch aggregation (accept if the one-minute fault visibility is met by a streaming path); storing every run in full for small tiers. Each is fine if saves are never blocked and chains are reconstructable.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Synchronous telemetry writes inside the save; unbounded buffers on application servers; sampling before counting, which breaks totals; chain context lost on asynchronous hops; field values leaking into fault messages; one org's loop flooding shared partitions and storage.

Incident guidance.

  • A loop produces 30% of runs, all stopped at {max_depth} levels: per-org quotas on the telemetry path keep other orgs' data flowing; aggregates still count every run exactly; keep full detail for a sample of the looping chains, not all of them; alert the administrator with the cycle of flows involved, derived from the chain tree.
  • Buffer full during a storage outage, four minutes of successes dropped: the drop counters say exactly how many runs per org and flow are missing; aggregates built upstream of the store (or from the counters) still show totals. Tell the administrator the window has no detail for successful runs; faults were in the priority buffer. Afterwards, size the buffer or spill to local disk.
  • Debug value capture never switched off: the platform should enforce expiry; here it did not. Stop the capture, delete the captured values beyond the session's intended window, notify the org's administrator, and treat it under the privacy incident process. Prevention: mandatory expiry, an alarm on long-running sessions and a review of every active session.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Record index lookup → chains that touched the account → the run that wrote the field → its parent chain back to the save. (2) Aggregates sliced by an attribute such as owner type or queue (a dimension of the record, not a value), plus full detail for every faulted run. (3) Detect loops from repeated (flow, record) pairs within a chain; cap detail; notify. (4) Count before sampling; percentiles from per-minute sketches of all durations, or from samples weighted by their inverse rate. (5) Compare versions by matched time windows and trigger types; watch for a different mix of records after deployment.

Rubric anchors. 2: write a log row per run synchronously; no chain ids; field values in the log. 3: non-blocking emission, chain and parent ids across async work, aggregates plus sampled detail with faults always kept, per-org isolation. 4: also exact counts under sampling, drop accounting, loop detection, audited and time-boxed value capture, and clear incident handling.

Strong signals. Says telemetry failure must not fail a save before designing storage; carries trace context through queued work. Red flags. Synchronous writes in the transaction; capturing record values by default; one shared table without org scoping.

SFC-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Policy, with valid time (the source of truth). Every table carries valid_from, valid_to (NULL = current) and the change event id that opened the row.
    • object_defaults (org_id, object, default_access private|read|read_write, hierarchy_access bool, valid_from, valid_to).
    • user_roles (org_id, user_id, role_id, active, valid_from, valid_to): a user's role and active state over time.
    • role_parents (org_id, role_id, parent_role_id, valid_from, valid_to) and a derived role_closure (org_id, ancestor_role_id, descendant_role_id, depth, valid_from, valid_to).
    • groups (group_id, kind public|role|role_and_subordinates, …), group_members (group_id, member_type user|role|role_and_subordinates|group, member_id, valid_from, valid_to) and a derived group_user_membership (group_id, user_id, valid_from, valid_to) resolved through the role closure and nested groups.
    • sharing_rules (rule_id, version, org_id, object, kind owner|criteria, source_group_id NULL, criteria_json NULL, target_group_id, access read|read_write, valid_from, valid_to): a stable rule_id plus a version per edit; a deleted and recreated rule is a new rule_id even with the same name.
    • record_owners (record_id, object, owner_user_id, valid_from, valid_to); manual_shares (share_id, record_id, principal_type, principal_id, access, valid_from, valid_to, end_reason owner_change|revoked); team_members (record_id, user_id, access, valid_from, valid_to).
    • criteria_field_history (record_id, field_id, value, valid_from, valid_to) only for fields that some criteria-based rule references, kept for the audit period; or, leaner, criteria_match_history (record_id, rule_id, rule_version, matched, valid_from, valid_to) so no field values are stored at all.
  • Derived access (a cache). record_access (record_id, principal_user_id, access, reason_type default|owner|hierarchy|rule|manual|team, reason_id, reason_version, valid_from, valid_to). It is computed incrementally from policy change events: a role move touches rows for records owned by users in the moved subtree and for users above it; a rule change touches records matching that rule. Each recalculation job has an id and a watermark; queries for a time beyond the watermark are answered from the policy tables directly or marked "recalculation in progress".
  • Point-in-time answer. WHERE record_id = R AND valid_from <= T AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > T) on record_access returns every grant path; the highest level is the max. The same question can always be recomputed from the policy tables (owner at T, owner's role at T, ancestors via closure at T, groups at T, rules at T with match state at T, shares and teams at T) — that recomputation is how the cache is verified.
  • Retention. Policy history (small) is kept for {{audit_years}} years in full. Derived rows can be compacted (merge adjacent intervals) or dropped beyond a few months and recomputed on demand from policy history; the policy history is what must never be shortened.
  • Cross-org analytics. Reads only policy metadata: counts of rules by kind, role tree depth, number of groups; never record ids, owners or field values; small categories suppressed.

Competing designs to accept. No derived table at all: compute access at query time from the temporal policy tables (fine for audit questions, slow for "which records could U see" in an org with {{org_records}} records unless the candidate bounds it). A derived table of current access only plus the temporal policy tables for history. Event sourcing of policy changes with periodic snapshots of the closure tables. Storing nested group membership as a materialised path instead of a closure table, if time-versioned.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A recursion over the current tree for a past date; a derived table with no reasons; rule identity by name; manual shares deleted on owner change so history is lost; storing full record contents to evaluate criteria; a reorg causing an org-wide rewrite (the worst case is records owned below the moved role × users above it — bound it and make it asynchronous with a visible watermark); membership history shorter than the audit requirement.

Incident guidance.

  • Reorg recalculation window: the derived rows were read as truth while incomplete. Contain by marking the report generated in the window as unreliable and re-issuing it from policy tables; tell the customer which report is superseded. Fix: every derived row set carries the recalculation watermark; queries for times past the watermark either wait, fall back to computing from policy, or are labelled. Guardrail: a reconciliation that samples records and compares derived access to a recomputation from policy at org scale ({{org_records}} records here).
  • Rule deleted and recreated with the same name: grants were keyed by name. Re-key derived grants to (rule_id, version), recompute the affected interval, and correct the answer that was given. Guardrail: a test that a recreated rule never inherits the old rule's history.
  • Membership history kept 90 days: the answer for grants via groups older than 90 days is UNKNOWN and must be stated as such, not guessed; reconstruct from any surviving audit trail of membership changes if it exists. Fix: retention of all policy history for {{audit_years}} years (it is small compared with records) and a retention test in the data contract.

Follow-up guidance. (1) 09:00: owner, default, hierarchy through the old managers. 12:00: hierarchy through the new managers only (closure at 12:00). 17:00: plus the Finance group through the criteria rule, because the record matched from 16:00. (2) Records owned by users in the moved subtree × users in the old and new ancestor chains; process it incrementally and expose the watermark. (3) Time-versioned closure tables; queries filter on validity at T. (4) Keep only the referenced fields' history, or only rule-match intervals; delete with the record. (5) Policy metadata counts only, aggregated, never record-level data.

Rubric anchors. 2: a current access table with a boolean, no history and no reasons. 3: temporal policy tables, derived access with reasons and validity, closure tables, point-in-time query defined. 4: also incremental recalculation with a visible watermark, rule identity by id and version, minimal criteria history, retention reasoning and metadata-only cross-org analytics.

Strong signals. Separates policy from derived access unprompted; asks how groups that contain roles move with the hierarchy. Red flags. Recursing over today's tree for a past date; rule names as keys; copying record contents to evaluate criteria.

SFC-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Metadata store.
    • objects (org_id, object_id) and object_versions (object_id, api_name, label, is_custom, deleted_state active|deleted|purged, valid_from, valid_to).
    • fields (org_id, object_id, field_id) and field_versions (field_id, api_name, label, data_type, length_or_precision, lookup_target_object_id NULL, formula_hash NULL, deleted_state, valid_from, valid_to, change_id).
    • picklist_values (field_id, value_id) and picklist_value_versions (value_id, api_value, label, active, sort_order, valid_from, valid_to).
    • schema_changes (change_id, org_id, kind add|rename|type_change|delete|restore|purge|picklist_change, entity_id, at, actor_id, deployment_id NULL): the event that opened each version.
    • Schema at time T: WHERE valid_from <= T AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > T). An API name is unique per (object, time), enforced with an exclusion constraint or a check at write time.
  • Customer export (per-org analytical tables). One defensible choice: per-org physical tables in the customer's own schema, with columns named by a stable mapping export_columns (org_id, field_id, column_name, column_type, created_at, retired_at). A rename changes only the mapping's display label (a view exposes friendly names); an API name reused by a new field gets a new column because its field_id differs. A type change creates a new column (e.g. region__v2) or a converted column with the old one retired, and a view presents the current shape; history is not silently cast. Delete hides the column in views; restore unhides; purge drops the column and its data in every copy, logged with a completion record per copy.
  • Alternatives for the pipeline. A wide table with typed generic slots per org (a slot allocator mapping field ids to text_07, num_12), attribute-value rows, or a semi-structured column. Each must show how a customer report with 40 fields over tens of millions of records is served (materialised wide views) and how type changes behave.
  • Cross-org metadata analytics. fct_org_schema_daily (snapshot_date, org_bucket, object_kind standard|custom, custom_field_count, field_type, deleted_within_30d_count) built from ids, types, counts and timestamps only; no api names, labels, descriptions or picklist values ever leave the org's metadata store. "Share of orgs with an object within 10% of the {{field_limit}} limit" = orgs with any object at ≥ 0.9 × {{field_limit}} custom fields ÷ all orgs, reported as a share with small cells suppressed; org ids are not in the product-facing table (or are pseudonymised and access-controlled).
  • Scale. {{schema_changes_per_day}} changes a day is small compared with record traffic, but arrives in bursts from deployments: process changes per org incrementally (only touched objects), batch a deployment's changes into one export migration.

Competing designs to accept. Generic slots or attribute-value storage for the export with materialised per-org views; JSON columns with a typed view per org regenerated on schema change; event-sourced metadata with snapshots. Any of these, if field identity is by id and purge reaches every copy.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. API names or labels as keys; ALTER TABLE storms at {{orgs}} orgs; casting historical values on type change; purge only in the primary store; cross-org pipelines that read labels or picklist values "just for statistics"; per-object field limits computed from current state only so deleted-but-restorable fields are miscounted (state the rule: in this exercise, deleted fields within the restore window still count toward the limit, or say which choice you make).

Incident guidance.

  • 300 fields deleted and re-created with the same API names: the export keyed on API names. Contain by freezing the customer's export and restoring the previous mapping; re-map history to the old field ids (now deleted) and start new columns for the new field ids; tell the customer which dashboards were affected. Guardrail: field id is the only join key; a test re-creates a field with a reused API name and checks history does not move.
  • Purge left copies: list every copy (export tables, staging, caches, backups with their expiry) in a purge registry; purge each and record completion; delete the staging table that captured picklist values and remove that capture from the pipeline. Guardrail: purge is complete only when every registered copy confirms; a scan of cross-org stores for value columns fails the build.
  • Dashboard with org ids and labels shared with a partner team: revoke access, remove labels from the product-facing table, report it through the privacy process, and rebuild the dashboard on bucketed shares with suppression. Guardrail: the cross-org model has no label or value columns at all, so the mistake cannot recur by query.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Two field ids: the old one now has api_name Territory__c; the new picklist has Region__c. The export keeps the old column (renamed in the view) and adds a new column. (2) New column or converted column with the old values kept; a saved report on old free text keeps working on history and shows unmapped values. (3) Delete hides, restore unhides with data, second delete and purge removes data everywhere; cross-org counts change only through type and count metrics. (4) Per org, max over objects of custom field count from field_versions at the date; share across orgs; suppression. (5) Process changes per org and object; purge registry with confirmations.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table per org altered in place, keyed by API name, labels used in analytics. 3: stable ids with versioned attributes, schema-as-of queries, a defended export layout with a mapping table, metadata-only analytics. 4: also purge propagation with proof, type-change handling that preserves history, burst handling and the label-as-customer-data reasoning.

Strong signals. Asks about API name reuse before designing; treats labels as customer data unprompted. Red flags. "Labels are just metadata, so they are fine to aggregate"; dropping history on a type change; purge implemented as a flag.

SFC-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Environments. environments (env_id, org_id, kind production|sandbox, sandbox_type NULL, source_env_id, created_at) and env_refreshes (refresh_id, env_id, source_env_id, requested_by, started_at, completed_at, source_state_as_of). A refresh is an event; the next allowed refresh is completed_at + {{refresh_days}} days in this exercise.
  • Components and versions. components (component_id, org_id, type, api_name); component_versions (version_hash, component_id, type, size_bytes, created_at) — the hash identifies content; the content itself stays in the org's metadata store, never in analytics.
  • Environment state. env_component_state (env_id, component_id, version_hash NULL for deleted, valid_from, valid_to, change_kind creation|deployment|direct|refresh|destructive, change_id). A refresh closes every interval of the sandbox and opens intervals copying production's state at source_state_as_of; the old intervals remain queryable.
  • Deployments. deployments (deployment_id, source_env_id NULL, target_env_id, requested_by, requested_at, kind validate|deploy|quick_deploy, validated_by_deployment_id NULL, reverses_deployment_id NULL, status queued|running|succeeded|failed|cancelled, finished_at); deployment_items (deployment_id, component_id, version_hash, action upsert|destructive); deployment_tests (deployment_id, test_id, outcome, duration_ms). Status comes from the outcome event, never from the request. Only a succeeded deploy opens state intervals.
  • Direct changes. setup_audit (audit_id, env_id, actor_id, at, change_type, component_id) plus the version hash read after the change; it opens a direct interval.
  • Drift. A production component whose current interval has change_kind = direct and opened after the last deployment of that component. Before a deployment, compare each item's component with production's current interval: if it is a drift interval, block or require acknowledgement.
  • Questions. Changes between T1 and T2: intervals of production with valid_from in [T1, T2), joined to deployments or audit entries for who and how. Which deployment introduced a version: the interval whose change_id is a deployment. Sandbox behind production: full outer join of current intervals by component_id where hashes differ, split into "changed in production since the sandbox's refresh" and "changed in the sandbox".
  • Rollback. A new deployment with reverses_deployment_id = X: for each component X upserted, the version in force before X (from state intervals); for each component X added, a destructive change. Data in a field that X added is lost if the field is deleted, so the reversing deployment needs an explicit approval and an export of that data first, or the field is kept and hidden.
  • Health analytics. fct_deployment (deployment_id, org_bucket, kind, status, component_type_counts, test_count, test_duration_ms, queued_ms, run_ms, failure_component_type), partitioned by day; at {{deployments_per_day}} a day this is small; retain for years. No component content, names or code.

Competing designs to accept. Snapshots of each environment's full manifest (component → hash) per change event, with diffs computed between snapshots, if they handle direct changes between snapshots via the audit trail. A source-control-centric design where the repository is the source of truth, as long as direct changes and drift are modelled. Event sourcing of state changes with materialised current state.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Nightly snapshots that miss same-day changes and their authors; status taken from the request; refresh overwriting sandbox history; rollback described as "restore the old org"; diffs over content instead of hashes; non-canonical serialisation making identical components hash differently (normalise before hashing); analytics reading customer code.

Incident guidance.

  • Integration sandbox refreshed before a release: from the closed intervals, list every component whose version in the sandbox differed from production at refresh time — that is the lost work, with hashes and authors; recover the content from the source sandboxes or the repository. Guardrail: a refresh request shows the pending-work diff and requires confirmation; automation cannot refresh an environment with undeployed changes; the {{refresh_days}}-day limit is shown before the refresh, not after.
  • Failed deployment recorded as deployed: correct the state by closing the wrongly opened intervals with a correction record (not a delete) and restoring the previous versions' intervals; status only from outcome events; a reconciliation that compares production's actual manifest with modelled state daily.
  • Hotfix overwritten: query deployments whose items replaced an interval with change_kind = direct, across the production org and its {{sandboxes_per_org}} sandboxes, for the quarter; report each with the hotfix and its author. Guardrail: the pre-deployment drift check.

Follow-up guidance. (1) env_component_state for the production env with valid_from in the range, joined to change sources. (2) Previous versions for changed components plus destructive changes for added ones; data consequences and approval. (3) The sandbox's closed intervals before the refresh versus production's state; a warning computed from that diff before refresh. (4) Drift interval detection before the deployment. (5) Success rate = succeeded deploys ÷ deploys attempted (excluding validations, or reported separately); test duration per component type; daily partitions.

Rubric anchors. 2: a list of deployments with no environment state, or nightly snapshots only, and rollback as "restore". 3: component-version intervals per environment, deployments with items and outcome status, direct changes in the same history, a rollback as a reversing deployment. 4: also drift detection before deploy, refresh lineage with lost-work reporting, canonical hashing and metadata-only health analytics.

Strong signals. Asks how direct production changes are seen before designing; distinguishes validation from deployment. Red flags. Taking status from the request; treating a refresh as an overwrite with no history; analytics on component content.

SFC-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Accounts and hierarchy. accounts (account_id, created_at) with account_versions (account_id, name, …, valid_from, valid_to); account_parent_history (account_id, parent_account_id NULL, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, change_kind normal|backdated). Valid time and recorded time are both kept, so a backdated change is visible (bitemporal).
  • Derived hierarchy. account_closure (ancestor_id, descendant_id, depth, valid_from, valid_to) or a path per account per version; ultimate_parent (account_id, global_parent_id, valid_from, valid_to) derived from it. Acyclicity and depth ≤ {{max_depth}} are checked when a parent link is ingested: a link that would create a cycle or exceed the depth is quarantined, never applied.
  • Contacts. contacts (contact_id, …); account_contact_relations (relation_id, contact_id, account_id, role, is_primary, valid_from, valid_to, end_reason ended|deleted|merged, restored_from_relation_id NULL). A deleted relationship closes with end_reason = deleted; a restore within 15 days opens a new interval linked to the deleted one (or reopens it, explicitly), so the gap is visible.
  • Merges. merges (merge_id, object account|contact, loser_id, survivor_id, merged_at, steward_id), merge_moves (merge_id, child_object, child_id, from_parent_id, to_parent_id). A resolved map merge_resolution (original_id, current_survivor_id, resolved_at) computed transitively (A → B → C resolves A to C); a merge whose survivor is already a loser is resolved at write time, and a merge that would create a cycle is rejected.
  • Facts. fct_opportunity_snapshot (snapshot_date, opportunity_id, account_id as recorded then, amount, stage, close_date): facts keep their original account id.
  • Rollups. As reported at date D: snapshot at D joined to ultimate_parent valid at D, with ids as they were at D (no merge resolution after D). Restated: the same snapshot, account ids re-pointed through merge_resolution and joined to the hierarchy as currently known for D (or today's hierarchy, stated). Both views carry a label and a computed-at time; a "differences" view explains the change per parent by cause (merge, hierarchy change, backdated change).
  • Scale. At {{accounts}} accounts and depth {{max_depth}}, the closure has at most accounts × depth rows per version; a re-parent of a subtree closes and opens rows for that subtree × the ancestors above it only.

Competing designs to accept. Materialised path strings per version instead of a closure; recursive queries at report time with a depth limit and cycle detection, if the hierarchy is small enough and point-in-time is respected; a type 2 dimension of account with a global-parent attribute recomputed on hierarchy change. Rewriting facts to survivors physically is acceptable only if the as-reported numbers are frozen elsewhere.
